claim: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of selected experiments from a number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of selected experiments from a number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as the purpose of the project.

claim: The papers selected for replication were published between 2010 and 2012.
source: The papers, which were published between 2010 and 2012, were selected on the basis of citations and Altmetric scores (Errington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract with citation to Errington et al., 2014.

claim: The papers were selected on the basis of citations and Altmetric scores.
source: The papers, which were published between 2010 and 2012, were selected on the basis of citations and Altmetric scores (Errington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract with citation to Errington et al., 2014.

claim: Poliseno et al. reported that microRNAs miR-19b and miR-20a transcriptionally suppress both PTEN and PTENP1 in prostate cancer cells.
source: In these experiments, Poliseno and colleagues report microRNAs miR-19b and miR-20a transcriptionally suppress both PTEN and PTENP1 in prostate cancer cells (Figure 1D; Poliseno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper by Poliseno et al., 2010, Figure 1D.

claim: Decreased expression of PTEN and/or PTENP1 resulted in downregulated PTEN protein levels.
source: Decreased expression of PTEN and/or PTENP1 resulted in downregulated PTEN protein levels (Figure 2H)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figure 2H.

claim: Decreased expression of PTEN and/or PTENP1 resulted in downregulation of both mRNAs.
source: downregulation of both mRNAs (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figure 2G.

claim: Decreased expression of PTEN and/or PTENP1 resulted in increased tumor cell proliferation.
source: increased tumor cell proliferation (Figure 2F; Poliseno et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figure 2F.

claim: Overexpression of the PTEN 3′ UTR enhanced PTENP1 mRNA abundance limiting tumor cell proliferation.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of the PTEN 3′ UTR enhanced PTENP1 mRNA abundance limiting tumor cell proliferation, providing additional evidence for the co-regulation of PTEN and PTENP1 (Figure 4A; Poliseno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figure 4A.

claim: PTEN functions as a negative repressor of the PI3K/Akt survival pathway.
source: The phosphatase and tensin homolog gene (PTEN) functions as a negative repressor of the PI3K/Akt survival pathway and is one of the most frequently deleted tumor suppressor genes in human cancer (Stambolic et al., 1998; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Stambolic et al., 1998 and Song et al., 2012.

claim: PTEN is one of the most frequently deleted tumor suppressor genes in human cancer.
source: The phosphatase and tensin homolog gene (PTEN) functions as a negative repressor of the PI3K/Akt survival pathway and is one of the most frequently deleted tumor suppressor genes in human cancer (Stambolic et al., 1998; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Stambolic et al., 1998 and Song et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of PTEN results in over-activation of Akt, leading to unchecked cell proliferation, reduced apoptosis, and elevated tumor angiogenesis.
source: As a regulator of PI3K signaling, loss of PTEN results in over-activation of Akt, leading to unchecked cell proliferation, reduced apoptosis, and elevated tumor angiogenesis (Stambolic et al., 1998; Carracedo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Stambolic et al., 1998 and Carracedo et al., 2008.

claim: In prostate cancer, decreases in PTEN protein expression can lead to invasive prostate carcinoma.
source: In prostate cancer, decreases in PTEN protein expression, either by allelic deletion or functional loss caused by mutation and/or epigenetic modification, can lead to invasive prostate carcinoma (Trotman et al., 2003; Phin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Trotman et al., 2003 and Phin et al., 2013.

claim: The genetic restoration of PTEN induces apoptosis in cancer cell lines.
source: In preclinical systems, the genetic restoration of PTEN induces apoptosis in cancer cell lines and has a significant negative effect on tumor growth in multiple in vivo models (Li et al., 1998; Lu et al., 1999; Tian et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Li et al., 1998; Lu et al., 1999; Tian et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2011.

claim: The genetic restoration of PTEN has a significant negative effect on tumor growth in multiple in vivo models.
source: In preclinical systems, the genetic restoration of PTEN induces apoptosis in cancer cell lines and has a significant negative effect on tumor growth in multiple in vivo models (Li et al., 1998; Lu et al., 1999; Tian et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Li et al., 1998; Lu et al., 1999; Tian et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Clinical efforts to restore PTEN functionality have focused on targeting kinases in the PI3K pathway, including PI3K, Akt, and the mammalian target of rapamycin.
source: In contrast, clinical efforts to restore PTEN functionality have instead focused on targeting kinases in the PI3K pathway, including PI3K, Akt, and the mammalian target of rapamycin (Hopkins and Parsons, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Hopkins and Parsons, 2014.

claim: The development of PI3K targeting drugs has been complicated by the limited tolerability of current pharmacological treatments as well as tumor heterogeneity.
source: However, the development of PI3K targeting drugs has been complicated by the limited tolerability of current pharmacological treatments as well as tumor heterogeneity (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Bauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gerlinger et al., 2012 and Bauer et al., 2014.

claim: MicroRNAs are small non-coding RNAs that bind to complementary sequences in the 3′ untranslated regions of target messenger RNAs, resulting in transcriptional downregulation of the target gene.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that bind to complementary sequences in the 3′ untranslated regions (UTR) of target messenger RNAs (mRNA), resulting in transcriptional downregulation of the target gene (Sen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Sen et al., 2014.

claim: PTEN was repressed by miR-21 in hepatocarcinoma cells.
source: Meng and colleagues showed that PTEN was repressed by miR-21, one of the most frequently upregulated miRNAs in cancer, in hepatocarcinoma cells, suggesting that the oncogenic potential of miR-21 occurs via the downregulation of PTEN expression (Chan et al., 2005; Meng et al., 2006; Volinia et al., 2006; Meng et al., 2007; Si et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Chan et al., 2005; Meng et al., 2006; Volinia et al., 2006; Meng et al., 2007; Si et al., 2007.

claim: miR-21 is one of the most frequently upregulated miRNAs in cancer.
source: Meng and colleagues showed that PTEN was repressed by miR-21, one of the most frequently upregulated miRNAs in cancer, in hepatocarcinoma cells, suggesting that the oncogenic potential of miR-21 occurs via the downregulation of PTEN expression (Chan et al., 2005; Meng et al., 2006; Volinia et al., 2006; Meng et al., 2007; Si et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Chan et al., 2005; Meng et al., 2006; Volinia et al., 2006; Meng et al., 2007; Si et al., 2007.

claim: The oncogenic potential of miR-21 occurs via the downregulation of PTEN expression.
source: Meng and colleagues showed that PTEN was repressed by miR-21, one of the most frequently upregulated miRNAs in cancer, in hepatocarcinoma cells, suggesting that the oncogenic potential of miR-21 occurs via the downregulation of PTEN expression (Chan et al., 2005; Meng et al., 2006; Volinia et al., 2006; Meng et al., 2007; Si et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion from the work of Meng and colleagues, with citations.

claim: Several miRNAs that target PTEN have been reported.
source: Several miRNAs that target PTEN have since been reported (Jackson et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Jackson et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: miRNAs themselves are subject to regulation by competing endogenous RNA species, including pseudogenes, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs.
source: While miRNAs play a functional role in silencing target gene expression, it is proposed that miRNAs themselves are subject to regulation by competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) species, including pseudogenes, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs (Salmena et al., 2011; Cesana and Daley, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal with citations to Salmena et al., 2011 and Cesana and Daley, 2013.

claim: In plants, the non-protein coding gene IPS1 sequesters miRNAs away from their mRNA targets, leading to an accumulation of target transcripts.
source: In plants, for example, the non-protein coding gene IPS1 sequesters miRNAs away from their mRNA targets, thereby leading to an accumulation of target transcripts (Franco-Zorrilla et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Franco-Zorrilla et al., 2007.

claim: Poliseno and colleagues proposed that pseudogenes can modulate parental gene expression by influencing the available levels of miRNAs within a cell.
source: Poliseno and colleagues proposed that pseudogenes, which are non-coding genomic DNA sequences closely related to parental genes, can modulate parental gene expression by influencing the available levels of miRNAs within a cell (Poliseno et al., 2010; Cesana and Daley, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal from Poliseno et al., 2010 and Cesana and Daley, 2013.

claim: The extent and manner that ceRNAs can exert a consequential effect on the repression of targets for that miRNA is currently unclear.
source: However, the extent and manner that ceRNAs can exert a consequential effect on the repression of targets for that miRNA is currently unclear (Broderick and Zamore, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Broderick and Zamore, 2014.

claim: Denzler and colleagues reported that the natural abundance of target sites exceeded miRNAs in adult mouse liver, making the ceRNA hypothesis unlikely.
source: Recently, Denzler and colleagues analyzed the stoichiometric relationship of miR-122 and target sites in adult mouse liver and reported that the natural abundance of target sites exceeded miRNAs, making the ceRNA hypothesis unlikely (Denzler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Denzler et al., 2014.

claim: PTENP1 is a pseudogene that shares close homology with PTEN, including the ability to bind miRNAs.
source: PTENP1 is a pseudogene that shares close homology with PTEN, including the ability to bind miRNAs (Fujii et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fujii et al., 1999.

claim: Overexpression of miR-19b and miR-20a in prostate cancer cells resulted in a significant decrease in PTEN and PTENP1 mRNA transcription.
source: As reported in Figure 1D, overexpression of miR-19b and miR-20a in prostate cancer cells resulted in a significant decrease in PTEN and PTENP1 mRNA transcription.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figure 1D.

claim: Overexpression of either miR-19b or miR-20a in cancer cell lines resulted in reduced PTEN mRNA levels and protein expression.
source: This is supported by additional studies demonstrating that overexpression of either miR-19b or miR-20a in cancer cell lines resulted in reduced PTEN mRNA levels and protein expression (Luo et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Luo et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014.

claim: The ability of miR-19b and miR-20a to target PTEN in prostate cancer was confirmed by Tay et al.
source: The ability of miR-19b and miR-20a to target PTEN in prostate cancer was further confirmed by Tay et al. (2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Tay et al., 2011.

claim: Downregulation of PTENP1 in DU145 prostate cancer cells resulted in a significant decrease in both PTEN and PTENP1 mRNA levels and protein expression.
source: Downregulation of PTENP1 in DU145 prostate cancer cells resulted in a significant decrease in both PTEN and PTENP1 mRNA levels and protein expression (Figure 2G-H; Poliseno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figures 2G-H.

claim: Downregulation of PTENP1 profoundly accelerated the proliferation of DU145 cells.
source: Furthermore, downregulation of PTENP1 profoundly accelerated the proliferation of DU145 cells (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figure 2F.

claim: Silencing of both PTEN and PTENP1 had an additive effect on DU145 cell proliferation.
source: with silencing of both PTEN and PTENP1 having an additive effect (Poliseno et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper.

claim: Downregulation of PTEN-ceRNAs CNOT6L and VAPA in prostate and colon cancer cells modulated PTEN expression, Akt activity, and cell growth.
source: Recently, Tay and colleagues reported that PTEN-ceRNAs, including CNOT6L and VAPA, phenocopied PTENP1 activity, as downregulation of these non-coding transcripts in prostate and colon cancer cells were also able to modulate PTEN expression, Akt activity, and cell growth (Tay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Tay et al., 2011.

claim: Other PTEN-ceRNAs that regulate PTEN expression have been reported in brain, breast, and skin cancers.
source: Additionally, other PTEN-ceRNAs that regulate PTEN expression have been reported in brain, breast, and skin cancers (Lee et al., 2010; Karreth et al., 2011; Sumazin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Lee et al., 2010; Karreth et al., 2011; Sumazin et al., 2011.

claim: PTENP1 antisense RNA has been reported to regulate PTEN transcription and mRNA stability.
source: Further to this, PTENP1 antisense RNA has been reported to regulate PTEN transcription and mRNA stability, suggesting a model where the PTENP1 pseudogene has biomodal functionality modulating PTEN (Johnsson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Johnsson et al., 2013.

claim: The PTENP1 pseudogene has biomodal functionality modulating PTEN.
source: Further to this, PTENP1 antisense RNA has been reported to regulate PTEN transcription and mRNA stability, suggesting a model where the PTENP1 pseudogene has biomodal functionality modulating PTEN (Johnsson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on findings from Johnsson et al., 2013.

claim: Overexpression of the PTEN 3′ UTR was found to de-repress PTENP1 expression and inhibited DU145 proliferation.
source: Poliseno and colleagues demonstrated that the PTEN 3′ UTR regulates pseudogene expression, since overexpression of the PTEN 3′ UTR was found to de-repress PTENP1 expression and inhibited DU145 proliferation (Figure 4A) (Poliseno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original paper, Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of either PTEN or PTENP1 suppressed renal cancer cell proliferation.
source: These results were also confirmed by experiments by Yu and colleagues showing that overexpression of either PTEN or PTENP1 suppressed renal cancer cell proliferation (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Yu et al., 2014.

claim: The oncosuppressive properties of overexpressing PTENP1 3′ UTR have been reported in various cancer cells.
source: Further to this, the oncosuppressive properties of overexpressing PTENP1 3′ UTR have been reported in various cancer cells (Poliseno et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Poliseno et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015.
